The width of the confidence intervals (CIs) reflects the growing uncertainty as the forecast horizon increases. Longer time horizons inherently have more room for variability related to random shocks or external influences, which leads to broader confidence intervals to account for this added uncertainty.

Specific risks or unexpected events could cause outcomes to fall outside the stated confidence intervals. In addition, structural breaks—such as a regime change in a system or a sudden change in how the data behaves—could invalidate the model's assumptions, making the forecast less reliable. Even seemingly minor events, like unmodeled seasonality or one-off anomalies, could push actual outcomes beyond the stated intervals, particularly at longer forecast horizons.
